To collect honey, you need to get a special jar from the questgiver by talking to her. Things to know, #1: The jar is valid within a limited quest area only; if you cross its border even a little, the jar and its contents disappear. Try to find the border first before losing honey. To fill the jar, you need to get up to the beehives, and "use"/frob them. Different hives give different amounts of honey; an status icon should appear with a number on it. Things to know, #2: The actual collection is only active during a specific quest phase "Gather honey for the Kodan", when a timer shows up. Outside that quest, you can still get the jar, do the jumping, but no honey is in the jar. So why can you get the jar when you can't effectively get honey? Officially, it's a bug. But if you go for some achievements, you need to activate/use/frob the hives, regardless of the honey. You can't do that without the jar. So this helps with the achievements, while frustrating players who don't know the special mechanics here. Depending on your other quests, a bee called Ms. Buzz can be found who asks you to give her the honey instead. If you do, she buzzes off and can be found in the "Queen's Confidence" location later. It's related to a different quest; no effect to the honey collection other than that. Now, the jumping puzzles can be quite taxing. There's a shortcut here, but it's kind of a spoiler: You can use the Jade Bot Glider Booster skill on "6" from EoD. Run up the hill a bit, jump downwards to glide, use booster to gain height. Booster takes 30 seconds to recharge.

If you don't know who has each diamond Step one Give each player a unique scoreboard ID. See this related question for how to do that. Step two Run the following command in a repeating, always active command block: execute as @e[type=item,nbt={Item:{id:"minecraft:diamond"}}] run data merge entity @s {Item:{components:{"minecraft:custom_data":{Unclaimed:1b}}}} This gives each diamond item on the ground a custom Unclaimed tag, allowing you implement Step 3 without 30+ command blocks per player Step three Once for each player who could be playing the map, run in a repeating command block: clear @a[scores={Id=1}] diamond[custom_data={Unclaimed:1b}] 1 and then, in a conditional chain command block that the repeating command block is pointing to /give @a[scores={Id=1}] diamond[custom_data={PlayerOwns:1b}] Repeat this for each player, using scores={Id=2} and PlayerOwns:2b for the second player and so on. Step four Now that each diamond has a tag describing whose it is, you can use the technique described in In2itivity's answer to determine who put a diamond in the chest. This has a known bug that if Alice puts a diamond in a container, and then Bob takes the diamond out of the container (and never drops and picks it up again), the diamond is still interpreted as belonging to Alice -- but I actually like that if I understand what you're doing correctly; if you stole someone else's diamond from a chest instead of mining your own, that means you're trying to cheat… karma! If you want a more seamless experience, you may want to interest yourself in player inventory modification . With the method above, the diamond is visibly replaced by a different one, you can use this to make a seamless replacement.

In Portal 1, these are "Advanced Knee Replacements" In-universe, they appear to make the user invulnerable to fall damage. According to the Wiki , In Portal 1, Chell uses 'Advanced Knee Replacements', until the explosion resulting from her defeat of GLaDOS at the end of the game broke them. In Portal 2 , Chell replaces them with a similar device, the "Long Fall Boot", explained in detail in this Aperture Science "Investment Opportunity" demonstration video: This video is part of a series of videos that were created to promote Portal 2, showcasing various bits of technology in the Portal universe as if it were actually Aperture Science seeking investors for their research & development. Note that both Portal 1 and Portal 2 are set after Aperture Science's demise Thus both the Advanced Knee Replacements and the Long Fall Boots, must have been made prior to those events. The reason for the replacement comes from the development of Portal 2. According to Matt Charlesworth , one of the people who worked on the game, the team debated keeping or replacing the 'Advanced Knee Replacement' in Portal 2, before eventually settling on the "Long Fall Boot" as a variant of the same technology.

You can beat the game and get any ending variation you wish from the first loop. But there's two sections in the endgame that get easier if you're not on the first loop: Your Signalscope will only show frequencies that you've already unlocked by finding an object that emits that signal. Finding the Vessel usually requires you to either track down an object on radio, or have already found it and marked it on your map. Speedrunners bypass this by simply knowing where it is. The helpful pop-up reminding you of the Eye Coordinates will only appear if you've legitimately seen those coordinates on a previous loop. If you only know the coordinates from out-of-game knowledge, you won't get the reminder but they'll still work. Loop counters, not affected by your actions except the number of loops that pass: You can only sleep at a fire to pass the time after the start of the third loop. The equipment in the Probe Tracking Module will count the number of loops elapsed. According to it, the game starts on loop 9,318,054. The easter egg scroll on Giant's Deep shows a "world line divergence" that changes over the course of the loops. The first loop has some important differences until you activate the statue and begin the game proper. You mentioned minor dialogue changes and the possibility to get a game-over by dying, but it's more than that. Time-sensitive events don't happen at all until you trigger the statue. If you somehow get onto your ship and into space without triggering the statue, you'll find that Brittle Hollow doesn't collapse, sand never flows off Ash Twin, and there's no time limit on your exploration. The loop starts from the beginning when you walk past the statue - even if it was broad daylight before, afterwards it'll be midnight on the first day. You usually don't notice this because the museum is indoors.

Short Answer: Enter the number "747" as the frequency to continue with the game. There is no way to find this information within the game (see full answer below). Full Answer: This is a question that one of my kids brought to me while playing the games that I grew up with, and - while you can find the following information on the internet - I thought it was worthy of documenting within Arqade. Interestingly, the method for getting the frequency has changed over the years. To be able to continue with the game requires knowledge of a 3-digit code that originally was included as a hidden message on a piece of paper that came with StarTropics when purchased new and unopened... 1990 Original NES Release From the original instruction manual: Notice the footnote in the bottom right corner: "Please read the letter from Dr. Jones appended to this booklet." Here is an image of the paper that was appended to the back ( image credit ): The basic gist of the letter is that Uncle Steve is responding to Mike and inviting him to visit him on C-Island. I will emphasize the extra words in the footnote at the bottom: "Note: This letter is very important so please hold onto it till the end of the game." As a kid, I remember thinking it was really cool to have this extra paper that was somehow important to the game. Now that we know about this physical letter, Baboo's cryptic message makes more sense. When the paper was made wet with water, a hidden message would appear ( image credit ): This was a real world component to a video game! Definitely a fun experience as a kid. Nowadays, you will likely buy the game used without the original packaging and manual - and crucial letter to Mike from Uncle Steve! The content of the secret message in the letter contributed to the whole secret spy feel: Uncle Steve felt as though he was being watched and took a precaution to put a "tiny transmitter in [his] shoe" which was tuned to the frequency of 747 MHz. 2008 Wii Virtual Console & 2016 Wii-U Virtual Console Releases When Nintendo released StarTropics for the Wii/Wii-U Virtual Console, they included an electronic version of the original letter in the Operations Guide, complete with a way to virtually "dip" the letter in water (by clicking on an image of a bucket of water) to reveal the necessary frequency: Here is a video of what it looked like to dip the letter on the Wii. (Thanks to @Showsni for the video link.) It is interesting to note that this virtual dipping only gave the minimum information to continue in the game (frequency 747 MHz), and did not include the hidden message from Uncle Steve revealing his (justified) paranoia and tiny transmitter. 2016 NES Classic Edition Release The NES Classic Edition release included two digital manuals, an " Electronic Manual " and a " Printed Manual ". The "Printed Manual" included the image of the blank letter. The "Electronic Manual" included a page to explain the letter and give the secret frequency: This gave all the same information as the original printed paper, complete with the secret message communicating Uncle Steve's spy-level precautions. 2019 Nintendo Switch Online Release When the game was released for the Nintendo Switch Online, they apparently omitted any copy of the letter (virtual, digital, or otherwise). Oops! Players who don't have any context to where that frequency was supposed to come from are forced to search online and find this answer: As we have learned from the above, the frequency that Nav-Com should tune to is 747 MHz. Entering this number will allow you to continue the game of StarTropics past Chapter 4.

This is the timeline of the games as we currently understand it † , according to official and unofficial sources : Main Timeline Skyward Sword ("Many years" later + 100 years) The Minish Cap ("Generations" later) Four Swords (After the Hylian civil war that lasted "a long time") Ocarina of Time / | \ Fallen Hero Timeline Child Timeline Adult Timeline ("Many years" later) A Link to the Past (Several months later) Majora's Mask ("Ages" + hundreds of years later) The Wind Waker (Soon after) Link's Awakening ("Many years" later) Twilight Princess (Soon after) Phantom Hourglass (Soon after) Oracle of Seasons/Ages (Hundreds of years later) Four Swords Adventures (One hundred years later) Spirit Tracks (Centuries later) A Link Between Worlds | | (Soon after) Triforce Heroes | | (An unknown amount of time later) Echoes of Wisdom * | | ("Many years" later) The Legend of Zelda | | (Six years later) The Adventure of Link | | (?)** (?)** (?)** Era of the Wilds/Great Calamity (Possibly more than 10,000 years later) Breath of the Wild * (Soon after) Tears of the Kingdom * The most confusing part is the timeline split after the events of Ocarina of Time . The quick explanation is that the Fallen Hero Timeline is the timeline where Link fails his quest and Ganon ends up with the completed Triforce, forcing the Sages to seal it and him within the Sacred Realm, which is now the Dark World. The Child Timeline is where Link successfully defeats Ganon and goes back in time as a child (i.e., the final scene of Ocarina of Time ). He warns Zelda about Ganondorf's betrayal and they prevent him from ever stealing the Triforce in the first place, though he survives his execution due to the gods giving him the Triforce of Power anyway ( for some reason ). The Adult Timeline stays in the future timeline after Link defeats Ganon. Because Link went back in time (to the Child Timeline), this timeline no longer has its Hero. So the next time Ganon appears, the gods are forced to intervene, resulting in the global flood. * : These games were released after the most recent official chronology update, so their place in the chronology is inferred from the in-game lore and might not be correct or might be retconned in the future. ** : It has been loosely confirmed that Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom take place at the end of one of the timelines, but which timeline specifically has apparently been left up to the imagination of the player . †: It is worth mentioning that according to The Legend of Zelda: Encyclopedia , the chronology of the Zelda games is not a high priority for Nintendo. They will maintain the timeline if practical, but they are also not afraid of breaking it for the sake of telling the story they want to tell for a specific game, and that ultimately the intention was always for the players themselves to create their own chronology according to their imagination. (Even the Encyclopedia itself states in its foreword that it was written with a certain amount of creative license to fill in some gaps.) So while the official timeline exists for the sake of convenience, it shouldn't be seen as an absolute truth.

Quake 3: Ray Traced (Q3RT) was released in 2004 by Daniel Pohl using the OpenRT library to demonstrate real-time ray tracing, but was mostly a research project. Demo: Retrospective research paper by the same author: Title: 15 Years Later: A Historic Look Back at "Quake 3: Ray Traced" Daniel Pohl, Selvakumar Panneer, Deepak Vembar, Carl Marshall . DOI: http://dx.doi.org/10.15439/2020F3 Citation: Proceedings of the 2020 Federated Conference on Computer Science and Information Systems, M. Ganzha, L. Maciaszek, M. Paprzycki (eds). ACSIS, Vol. 21, pages 401–412 (2020) Abstract: Real-time ray tracing has been a goal and a challenge in the graphics field for many decades. With recent advances in the hardware and software domains, this is becoming a reality today. In this work, we describe how we got to this point by taking a look back at one of the first fully ray traced games: Quake 3: Ray Traced . We provide insight into the development steps of the project with unreleased internal details and images. From a historical perspective, we look at the challenges pioneering in this area in the year 2004 and highlight the learnings in implementing the system, many of which are relevant today. We start by going from a blank screen to the full ray traced gaming experience with dynamic animations, lighting, rendered special effects and a simplistic implementation of the gameplay with basic AI enemies. We describe the challenges encountered with aliasing and the methods used to alleviate it. Lastly, we describe for the first time the unofficial continuation of the project, code named Quake 3: Team Arena Ray Traced , and provide an overview of the changes over the past 15 years that made it possible to generate fully ray-traced interactive gaming experiences with mass market hardware and an open software stack.

It's complicated, and I have not developed a complete understanding of it in my trip down this rabbit hole, but I would like to document what I have learned in this answer. First, it's good to understand more precisely what the question is about. When you hover a game on the main store page, you get a little info card about the game: What do those icons mean? Looking at the HTML gives us the file names of those icons: ico_singlePlayer.png , ico_multiPlayer.png and ico_coop.png . If you look at the store page for a game, there is an info section for the game that features those same icons (this one being from Project Zomboid as well): But as you can see, while the info section use the same icons, it does not have a matching number of them, meaning the hover list is not simply a reproduction of the info section. The mystery deepens further when you realise some games show the multiplayer icon without having an info section entry using it (example: Fast Food Simulator), and others show the Co-op icon without a Co-op entry (example: Hearts of Iron IV). The latter one provided a clue. How is Hearts of Iron IV associated with Co-op? The answer turns out to be that Co-op is one of the popular user defined tags for it: This is the only thing relating to Co-op I can find on that game's store page, leading me to believe that the extra icons correspond to tags. Annoyingly the tags don't show these icons, so exactly which tags are associated with which icons is a detail buried in Steam's code base. Cutting out the gory details of all the games I looked at to piece this together, my current model is that this sequence of icons will be, in order: A single player icon, if the game features a single player mode A multiplayer icon, if the game features any form of multiplayer A sequence of zero or more multiplayer icons corresponding to tags and info section entries A sequence of zero or more co-op icons corresponding to tags and info section entries A multiplayer icon, if the game features cross platform multiplayer Points of unclarity being which tags are relevant, and whether there are any other obscure factors that could stick an icon somewhere in the sequence. But this matches all of the games I've looked at, at least. When turning on your controller, hold down L1 + A and then (while the other buttons are still held) press Steam , to go into its second pairing slot (this appears to be the information the Steam help page is missing). Your controller will make a different to normal noise when it turns on; the different noises are meant to help denote what device the controller is going to attempt to pair to. Then follow the pairing instructions in the question. The controller will now pair to the device and use the Puck/Steam Machine as the 2nd device. You can then see the 2 paired devices in your Steam Settings, under Controller, while the Controller is turned on: In the future, you should hold the relevant buttons when turning on the controller to connect to the correct device. R1 + A , Steam to connect to your primary device (the Steam Machine in this example), and L1 + A , Steam for the secondary (the Puck attached to the PC in this example). The controller will, however, remember what pairing slot it was last in if you simply turn it on with the Steam button. So, if you were last using your controller with your Puck, turning it on with the Steam button will mean it'll attempt to pair to the second device (the Puck). Again, the noise the controller makes will help you identify what device it will try to pair to. You need to turn the controller off (hold the Steam button), and and turn it back on with the correct button combination to change pairing slot. Note, you can also use R1 + B , Steam to enable Bluetooth pairing. Of course, pairing with Bluetooth doesn't follow the above instructions as this doesn't use a Puck.

Using different BIL (windbomb) methods is mostly preference, but there are some benefits to using each. The square bomb has a flatter surface area, thus giving you more room for error. The round bomb has a rounded surface area which means you need to hit it more directly into link. For this reason, most people use the round bomb first so as to impact the square bomb into link. The square bomb is used first in some setups with the main one being off the ground, such as the backflip setup, in which you use a stump/elevated surface to get bullet time from a backflip towards the square bomb, pulling out the circle bomb midair and detonating the square, with a consistent circle bomb impact into you. People who learn the stump method first will often use the square bomb first as it feels more natural, or use the square first as their tutorial did so. I also believe that square first can be better for vertical gliding BILs as you will have a better diagonal than the square's corner, because every direction from the circle is equal, you can go up or down further. Using the circle first is much easier for ledge and spider BILs, and I will recommend that you start using it first. I would say for learning BIL, you will want to start with the spider, then ledge, followed by horizontal gliding BIL. The vertical gliding BIL you learn when you have higher stamina and you have the stamina to chain a vertical gliding into a horizontal gliding, just to be able to get anywhere faster, scale cliffs, or just glide longer.

Gachas are characterized by the fundamental way some, or all, of gameplay is gated: by a lootbox-adjacent mechanic. The difference between gachas and, say, Counter-Strike 2's lootboxes is that you may play all of what Counter-Strike 2 has to offer without ever opening a box, and not in a "technically, if you grind for 234 hours, you will be able to afford [weapon] for free" kind of way. The only things that are locked behind a loot box (however expensive it is to open) in Counter-Strike 2 are entirely cosmetic. For contrast, take the quintessential "gacha game": Genshin Impact. In Genshin Impact, to be able to play in a certain way, such as playing as a certain character, or using a certain weapon, the only way is to open a loot box. You may not buy the character from the shop directly. The only way to get what you want is to gamble. Sure, there are ways of gambling for free built into the game (this is a player retention mechanic, gachas are necessarly full of them otherwise they'd be extremely frustrating), but the fundamentals don't change: in order to experience the full game, or indeed any of the game at all, you must gamble. Some would argue that the entire purpose of the game is the gambling. Dragon Collection, one of the original gachas, was actually literally just a collection game with no gameplay attached. The entire point was to gamble to get the dragon you're missing from your collection. It was quite successful for a browser game of the era. Of course, this is a spectrum. Some games can be located somewhere in the middle, where most of the gameplay can genuinely be accessed for free, but the truly powerful elements are behind a lootbox wall. Also note that gacha games are not to be confused with so-called "freemium" games, where the game favors paid players much more than free-to-play ones. While the two are obviously related, the difference mostly comes down to the fact that freemium games almost always guarantee you will obtain something powerful by paying every time, while gachas hold no such guarantees and can very well reward you with "filler" items even after paying. In conclusion, gachas are defined not by "some amount of randomness in terms of player rewards", but large amounts of randomness in access to gameplay to begin with.

At the time this question was asked, the answer would have been affected by even more randomness, because there used to be a random tick delay after mining most ores which was removed on December 7th 2022 . Official messaging indicating that: Get your Pickaxes at the ready, because we’ve removed the delay after Mining Copper, Tin, Coal, Blurite, Silver, Volcanic Ash, Gem Rocks, Gold, Mithril, Lovakite, Adamantite, Clay, Salts, Runite and Amethyst. Phew, we can take a breath now. First, the factors affecting your chance to obtain ore from mining are as you noted, with one addition: Pickaxe material, which determines how many ticks there are between rolls to obtain an ore Mining level, which determines what ores you can mine and the odds of obtaining an ore when rolling. Note that any bonuses to mining level such as the hidden Mining Guild boost will increase your odds of obtaining an ore based on your effective level, but not allow you to mine new ores. Ore being mined, which also determines the odds of obtaining ore when rolling. Mining enhancers , which can add a chance to obtain an extra ore when rolling, among some other effects that do not directly impact ore rates. With these factors in mind, here's my stab at an actual formula for ores per hour. First, variables, constants, and their sources: There are 0.6 seconds per game tick : The game tick, also known as the server cycle, is the fundamental unit of time used in Old School RuneScape, equal to 0.6 seconds. All actions that require server processing are governed by this value. Each pickaxe rolls to obtain ore from a rock every n ticks, where n is determined by the specific pickaxe being used . Note that the Dragon, Infernal, 3rd Age, and Crystal pickaxes actually have a chance to take one fewer tick, but we'll use the average as the wiki does. Better picks do not increase mining odds, only frequency. Higher-level pickaxes grant more frequent opportunities to obtain an ore from a rock but do not impact the success rate of doing so. 3 ticks by default, 1/6 chance to be 2 ticks [for the Dragon, Infernal, and 3rd Age pickaxes]. 3 ticks by default, 1/4 chance to be 2 ticks [for the Crystal pickaxe]. And there is a certain chance to obtain an ore per roll, which depends on the mined ore and your mining level. For simplicity, we'll assume that this percentage of rolls will yield an ore. Unfortunately for our purpose, while there are formulas for each rock type that determine your percent chance to obtain an ore on each roll, these formulas are not publicly known! Some have been derived and posted on the wiki , but all of them seem to be unrelated to one another. For example, your odds of obtaining Silver ore each roll at level 20 is 60/256 (23.44%), and 199/256 (77.73%) at level 99, with increases in those odds at every level. However, for Runite, your odds are 17/256 (6.64%) at level 85, and 19/256 (7.42%) at level 99, with increases every 6 levels (at 91 and 97). In short, we just have to look up the odds for each ore at each mining level. So the formula, which assumes perfect mining: time spent mining t / 0.6 seconds per tick = ticks ticks / ticks per roll (from pickaxe) = rolls rolls * ore chance per roll (from level and ore) = expected ore yield expected ore yield * (1 + odds of obtaining an extra ore per roll) = actual ore yield ((t time spent mining / 0.6 seconds/tick) / (n ticks/roll)) * p1 ore chance * (1 + p2 extra ore chance) = ore yield So for example, if you mine iron with level 55 mining , you have a 237/256 (92.58%) chance to obtain an ore. If you mine iron for an hour using a Rune pickaxe (3-tick), you'll roll for ore 2000 times and obtain an ore 92.58% of the time, and so expect to obtain ~1850 ores. If you've completed the Varrock easy diary and use the Varrock armour 1 while mining, you have a 10% chance to get an extra ore on each successful roll, so you'd expect to obtain ~2035 ores instead. ((1hr / 0.6seconds/tick) / (3 ticks/roll)) * 237/256 ore chance * (1 + 0.10 extra ore chance) = ~2036 ores per hour. Not bad! Except this doesn't consider banking time, or how quickly your inventory will fill up with non-ore items like gems (especially with bonuses from the amulet of glory !) or unidentified minerals from the Mining Guild . To consider these factors in a general way, we can introduce an efficiency percentage , which will be the percent of time spent actively mining during a period of time in which you're generally participating in mining but leave occasionally to bank your loot. I can't provide a direct way to calculate this percentage, as it will depend on how quickly you can navigate to the nearest bank and how often your inventory fills up. But it's easy to introduce: ((t time spent mining / 0.6 seconds/tick) / (n ticks/roll)) * k efficiency * p1 ore chance * (1 + p2 extra ore chance) = ore yield So if we continue the prior example, sneak into the Mining Guild with a Spicy Stew boost of +5 , and assume that 20% of our time is spent banking (or conversely, 80% of our time is spent mining), we can take advantage of the cluster of three iron rocks and being steps from a deposit box . In this circumstance, and adjusting for our 80% efficiency, you'd expect to obtain ~1628 iron ore. Well, except that our effective level is now 62 because of the invisible +7 boost to mining from the mining guild , so our ore chance goes up to 255/256 (99.61%) . Re-entering this into the formula to update our result: ((1 hour spent mining / 0.6 seconds/tick) / (3 ticks/roll)) * 0.80 efficiency * (255/256) ore chance * (1 + 0.1 extra ore chance) = ~1753 ores per hour. Given the iron mining guide from before defaults to 1700 iron ore per hour for calculating your profit, I'm reasonably confident this figure is accurate to the given circumstances.

No, not necessarily at Y 127 According to Minecraft Wiki , When lightning is to strike, random X and Z coordinates within the chunk are chosen, and the block just above the highest block that is liquid or obstructs movement is chosen for the lightning strike. If a lightning rod is nearby, it strikes the rod instead. Then if there are any living entities that can see the sky in a 3×h×3 region from 3 below the target block up to the world height, one such entity is selected at random and the lightning target is moved to the block the entity stands in. The target block is checked again for the following conditions: Target block can see the sky. Rain (not snow) is falling in the target block. Thus, lightning does not naturally strike within cold biomes or biomes where it does not rain. If these conditions pass, lightning strikes. That means it will strike as long as the block can see the sky (the path of the lighting isn't impeded by another block). So if you build a roof at Y=256, and it's the highest non-air block in that column, then yes, lightning will hit that roof instead of your house below. Building a glass roof at Y=256 will protect everything underneath, as long as it's the highest surface. You don’t need to build it at Y=126 — that’s not a special lightning layer. If you want more control, use a lightning rod : It attracts lightning within a ~64-block radius (Java). Place it somewhere safe, and it’ll redirect lightning strikes away from flammable structures. TL;DR: No, lightning doesn’t strike only at Y=127. It hits the highest block in the column. A roof at Y=256 will absolutely stop lightning from hitting your house below.

I ran into this problem and couldn't find a solution online. Later I managed to find a fix so I'm sharing it here in hope it can help other Blizzard game players playing on NVIDIA GeForce Now. This is for people with multiple battle.net accounts, playing Blizzard games using NVIDIA GeForce Now, needing to switch battle.net accounts on GeForce Now, who have trouble using the automatic login feature to log into the correct battle.net account as they have set, where GeForce Now may be logging them into a previously connected battle.net account. After trial and error, here's how I fixed it: First disconnect any Battle.net account from your GeForce Now settings. Then in your browser go to "account.battle.net" and log into your old account. On the left side menu, go to "Connections", and you should see this: "NVIDIA GeForce Now" is in Connections, as well as "Authorized Applications" down bottom. You want to remove both of these from your old account. (After that, I waited a few moments. I'm not sure if this is necessary, but I wanted to be on the safe side. In fact I would recommend waiting a few moments between some of the steps just to prevent any possible syncing issues) Log your old battle.net account out from the browser, and log your new one in. Go to GeForce Now and connect your new battle.net account like normal. Launch the game from GeForce Now. Once the game window opens, you should already be logged out of any battle.net accounts, and will be prompted to connect one. You just connect your new one there. Hopefully this can help people!

To pair your controller with a second Puck or Steam Machine and use it as a second device, you need to ensure that your controller is turned on in its second pairing slot. When turning on your controller, hold down L1 + A and then (while the other buttons are still held) press Steam , to go into its second pairing slot (this appears to be the information the Steam help page is missing). Your controller will make a different to normal noise when it turns on; the different noises are meant to help denote what device the controller is going to attempt to pair to. Then follow the pairing instructions in the question. The controller will now pair to the device and use the Puck/Steam Machine as the 2nd device. You can then see the 2 paired devices in your Steam Settings, under Controller, while the Controller is turned on: In the future, you should hold the relevant buttons when turning on the controller to connect to the correct device. R1 + A , Steam to connect to your primary device (the Steam Machine in this example), and L1 + A , Steam for the secondary (the Puck attached to the PC in this example). The controller will, however, remember what pairing slot it was last in if you simply turn it on with the Steam button. So, if you were last using your controller with your Puck, turning it on with the Steam button will mean it'll attempt to pair to the second device (the Puck). Again, the noise the controller makes will help you identify what device it will try to pair to. You need to turn the controller off (hold the Steam button), and and turn it back on with the correct button combination to change pairing slot. What was the first game to voluntarily provide an in-game content warning? What was the first game to voluntarily provide an in-game content warning? If you grew up playing horror games, you've probably seen content warnings similar to this: This one is from Silent Hill , published in 1999. Basically, it's a voluntary self-declaration by the game that there's something objectionable presented in the game. What I'm looking for: The first voluntary message in a game outside of the game's internal narrative that warns the player about morally objectionable content in the game's story or presentation. Objectionable content is very commonly violent or sexual in nature, but it doesn't have to be. ( Assassin's Creed , for example, self-declared that its story could be considered culturally offensive.) The content warning could also be done tongue-in-cheek so long as it still performs the service of a content warning. (For example, God Hand featured a content warning for explicit violence and gore, which it certainly had, but it was first and foremost a jab at the content warnings at the beginning of Resident Evil games, which shared directors and publishers. It was also overlaid over a man getting kicked in the balls.) What I'm not looking for: Standardized warnings/descriptions required by government or commercial entities (ESRB, Videogame Rating Council, etc.). For the sake of having a tight upper bound, we won't accept anything required by the platform manufacturer. So, as in the above, a warning internally mandated by Konami for all Silent Hill games can be considered, but a warning required by Sony for all PlayStation 2 games cannot. In-game characters warning about objectionable content (for example, protestors in Postal 2 that object to events in the game). Warnings that focus on meta gameplay aspects rather than morally objectionable content (for example, Doom 's Nightmare difficulty displaying the message "Are you sure? This skill level isn't even remotely fair."). Warnings provided by advertisements, box art, cabinet art, and so forth. It has to be in the game.

This is the timeline of the games as we currently understand it † , according to official and unofficial sources : Main Timeline Skyward Sword ("Many years" later + 100 years) The Minish Cap ("Generations" later) Four Swords (After the Hylian civil war that lasted "a long time") Ocarina of Time / | \ Fallen Hero Timeline Child Timeline Adult Timeline ("Many years" later) A Link to the Past (Several months later) Majora's Mask ("Ages" + hundreds of years later) The Wind Waker (Soon after) Link's Awakening ("Many years" later) Twilight Princess (Soon after) Phantom Hourglass (Soon after) Oracle of Seasons/Ages (Hundreds of years later) Four Swords Adventures (One hundred years later) Spirit Tracks (Centuries later) A Link Between Worlds | | (Soon after) Triforce Heroes | | (An unknown amount of time later) Echoes of Wisdom * | | ("Many years" later) The Legend of Zelda | | (Six years later) The Adventure of Link | | (?)** (?)** (?)** Era of the Wilds/Great Calamity (Possibly more than 10,000 years later) Breath of the Wild * (Soon after) Tears of the Kingdom * The most confusing part is the timeline split after the events of Ocarina of Time . The quick explanation is that the Fallen Hero Timeline is the timeline where Link fails his quest and Ganon ends up with the completed Triforce, forcing the Sages to seal it and him within the Sacred Realm, which is now the Dark World. The Child Timeline is where Link successfully defeats Ganon and goes back in time as a child (i.e., the final scene of Ocarina of Time ). He warns Zelda about Ganondorf's betrayal and they prevent him from ever stealing the Triforce in the first place, though he survives his execution due to the gods giving him the Triforce of Power anyway ( for some reason ). The Adult Timeline stays in the future timeline after Link defeats Ganon. Because Link went back in time (to the Child Timeline), this timeline no longer has its Hero. So the next time Ganon appears, the gods are forced to intervene, resulting in the global flood. * : These games were released after the most recent official chronology update, so their place in the chronology is inferred from the in-game lore and might not be correct or might be retconned in the future. ** : It has been loosely confirmed that Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom take place at the end of one of the timelines, but which timeline specifically has apparently been left up to the imagination of the player . †: It is worth mentioning that according to The Legend of Zelda: Encyclopedia , the chronology of the Zelda games is not a high priority for Nintendo. They will maintain the timeline if practical, but they are also not afraid of breaking it for the sake of telling the story they want to tell for a specific game, and that ultimately the intention was always for the players themselves to create their own chronology according to their imagination. (Even the Encyclopedia itself states in its foreword that it was written with a certain amount of creative license to fill in some gaps.) So while the official timeline exists for the sake of convenience, it shouldn't be seen as an absolute truth.

Baldur's Gate 3 includes all 12 principal base classes that have been around for at least two editions (the Warlock, being the newest entry, was introduced during 3.5, and turned core for the 4th edition), and have been published as such in the 5th edition Player's Handbook. With the subclasses it's a bit more complicated: BASE CLASS 5E core [2014] BG3 BG3 Patch 8 Barbarian 2: Path of the Berserker, Path of the Totem Warrior 3: Berserker, Wildheart, Wild Magic Path of the Giant Bard 2: College of Lore, College of Valour 3: College of Lore, College of Valour, College of Swords College of Glamour Cleric 7 Domains: Knowledge, Life, Light, Nature, Tempest, Trickery, War 7: idem Extra domain: Death Druid 2: Circle of the Land, Circle of the Moon 3: Circle of the Land, Circle of the Moon, Circle of the Spores Circle of Stars Fighter 3: Champion, Battle Master, Eldritch Knight 3: idem Arcane Archer Monk 3: Way of the Open Hand, Way of Shadow, Way of the Four Elements 3: idem Way of the Drunken Master Paladin 3 (4): Oath of Devotion, Oath of the Ancients, Oath of Vengeance 4: idem + Oathbreaker (but mentioned in DMG 5E) Oath of the Crown Ranger 2: Hunter, Beast Master 3: Hunter, Beast Master, Gloom Stalker Swarmkeeper Rogue 3: Thief, Assassin, Arcane Trickster 3: idem Swashbuckler Sorcerer 2: Wild Magic, Draconic Bloodline 3: idem + Storm Sorcery Shadow Magic Warlock 3: The Archfey, The Fiend, The Great Old One 3: idem Hexblade Wizard 8 Schools: Abjuration, Conjuration, Divination, Enchantment, Evocation, Illusion, Necromancy, Transmutation 8: idem Bladesinging Most of the additional subclasses from the game, including those from Patch 8 , have been published in the supplementary 5E sourcebooks: the Bard subclasses College of Swords and College of Glamour , the Ranger subclass Gloom Stalker , the Sorcerer subclasses Storm Sorcery and Shadow Magic , the Fighter's Arcane Archer , the Monk's Drunken Master , the Rogue's subclass Swashbuckler , and the Warlock subclass Hexblade were published in Xanathar's Guide to Everything , and the Druid's Circle of the Spores and Circle of Stars , the Barbarian's Wild Magic , the Ranger's Swarmkeeper , and the Wizard's Bladesinging in Tasha's Cauldron of Everything . Patch 8's Paladin subclass Oath of the Crown originates in the Sword Coast Adventurer's Guide and the Barbarian subclass Path of Giants in Bigby Presents - Glory of the Giants (as Path of the Giant ). The only two outliers here are the Barbarian's subclass Wildheart , which is Larian's reinterpretation of Path of the Totem Warrior (see e.g. here ), and the Cleric's Death Domain that was added by Patch 8, which is actually a core subclass (from the Dungeon Master's Guide). As for the Artificer base class: this was introduced in the Eberron campaign setting, already during the 3rd edition (but as a Wizard specialization already as far back as 2E), and made its reappearance during the 4th and 5th in non-core rulebooks. As jwodder points out in their answer , it was published in Tasha's Cauldron of Everything , which is a sourcebook (expanding on the Player's Handbook , Dungeon Master's Guide , and the Monster Manual ). Tasha's Cauldron of Everything was published in 2020, whereas development on Baldur's Gate 3 already started in 2016: apart from the exclusion of the Artificer base class from the core rulebooks, this could account for this class not having made it into the game. You will need a scoreboard objective. I called it 'testing' here: /scoreboard objectives add testing dummy Then whenever you want to check, run this command chain: /execute store result score day testing run time query day /scoreboard players set operand testing 8 /scoreboard players operation day testing %= operand testing This will get the current day count ( /time query day ) and store it in a virtual player score day . Then it will get the 'modulus 8' of that number, which means it'll get the remainder when dividing the number by 8. Doing this makes the day count loop from 0 -> 7. In Minecraft, there are effectively 8 days in a week. You can then do certain commands on certain 'weekdays' with the command /execute if score day testing matches <x> run <y> where x is the day and y is the command to be ran. 0 is a full moon, and 4 is a new moon.

When fighting against Grey Prince Zote, the best advice I can give you is to try and stay as close to him as possible so that you know what he's up to, while trying to keep a safe distance because, as you mention, his nail has a very long reach. It's counter intuitive because staying far away from the boss/threat should make you safe, but if the boss is out of your line of sight, you have no idea what they'll do next. Specifically in the case of Zote, keeping him in your line of sight helps in 3 kind of situations (timestamps based on your video): At 1:11 in your video, he does his huge leap then slam his nail onto the ground. Even if you stand very far, this leap will get close enough to surprise you, and since you don't see him making the initial leap, it can take you by surprise, like at 1:28, whereas if you're at point blank like at 0:45 and 0:56, you can dodge it nearly the same way as one of his normal jumps. Another danger is when he "teleports" into the sky like at 0:58. If you're too far, you won't know he's going to fall into you unless you recognise his scream, whereas if you keep him in range, you will notice him disappearing, allowing you to mentally prepare to dodge him from above. You probably noticed you can tell from which direction he's falling based on where the scream comes from (left, right, or right where you are). And in the case of his frantic swing, you need to find a middle ground: if you stand too close, the moment he raises his nail with its long reach, you may be hit even before you get to dodge it. But if you stand too far, he may have too much acceleration for you to have enough time to dodge it. As you can see at 1:16 in your video, he starts out slowly and quickly becomes very fast. But every time you go to the other side, he has to resume accelerating. The trick here is: when you dodge him/jump over him and land on the other side, you can see he still has some momentum when he turns around to try and keep chasing you, a bit like a car doing a U-turn: it needs to stop before it can go the other way. Basics of commands and arguments Minecraft's commands system allows players to modify the game in ways besides mining and placing blocks. Commands have different arguments that specify their behavior, such as a selected entity or specified location. For example, the very basic version of /summon has two arguments: An entity to summon A location to summon it at It is important to note that the term “entity” does not only refer to mobs, such as creepers and blazes, but also to other objects that are not blocks, including item frames, paintings, snowballs, and dropped items. Knowing the /summon command's arguments, we can fill them in like so: Example Summon a wither skeleton at the position (0, 80, 0). summon minecraft:wither_skeleton 0 80 0 Relative and local coordinates This, however, is very limiting: what if we wanted to summon an entity at our current position? This is where relative cordinates come in. Relative coordinates are used by putting a ~ instead of a number. To summon a silverfish at my current location, you would do /summon minecraft:silverfish ~ ~ ~ . If you want to add an offset to the location of the relative coordinates, you can do so by typing numbers directly after the ~ . Example To summon a lightning bolt 1 block east, 2.3 blocks up, and 17.914 blocks north: summon minecraft:lightning_bolt ~1 ~2.3 ~-17.914 There are also local coordinates , which use carets ( ^ ^ ^ ). These work identically to relative coordinates, but any offset you use is offset based on the direction that the executing entity is looking. Example Summon a fireball one block in front of the executing entity's crosshairs: summon minecraft:fireball ^ ^ ^1 You cannot mix local coordinates with other types of coordinates. All three axes X, Y, and Z must either all use ^ or not . Target selectors Alongside positional coordinates, which select a position in the world to work with, there are also arguments which select an existing entity within the world to work with. These are named target selectors , but can be called entity selectors as an alternative name. The most basic entity selector is simply the @ sign followed directly by one of five letters. There are five options: @s selects the self (the entity executing the command) @p selects the closest player (to the executing position) @r selects a random player in the world @a selects all players in the world @e selects all entities in the world Target selectors also accept arguments , which are filters to further narrow the amount of entities selected. These range from selecting entities based on what type of entity they are, to filtering based on their location, or even based on their name, or the number of XP levels they have. Selectors are useful if you want to do anything to anyone besides named players: Analysis kill @e[type=minecraft:item] The command is /kill . /kill accepts a single argument, an entity selector that selects which entity to kill. The target selector is @e[type=minecraft:item] . The @e says to start with a list of all entities. Then, type=minecraft:item filters the list to only include item entities and nothing else. All entities that are within the list after filtering will be killed. Therefore: This command will kill all entities of type minecraft:item . This means that all dropped item entities will be killed. It is at this point that it should be noted that commands are case-sensitive. This means that you cannot put a capital letter where there should be lowercase, or vice versa. Many broken commands have been fixed by correcting a misplaced capital or lowercase letter, so make sure you are always very careful about what you are typing. Because there are so many different selector arguments, we won't be covering them all here. If you would like to see what's available, click the link above to view a full list on the Minecraft Wiki. That being said, we have a few important things to note: x= , y= , and z= are special arguments. They are different from the rest in that they are not actual filters, but they instead provide information to other filters. x= , y= , and z= define a position in the world where the other filters are calculated from. Analysis kill @a[x=1,y=2,z=3] The command is /kill . /kill accepts one argument, an entity or list of entities to remove. The target selector is @a[x=1,y=2,z=3] . The only filters present are x=1,y=2,z=3 , defining a position for other filters to be calculated from. But there are no other filters that will utilize this position. Therefore: The target selector @a[x=1,y=2,z=3] does not perform any filtering. This command will kill all players in the dimension that you run this command from. /execute command This is all very useful, but how would I go about summoning a lightning bolt onto every creeper in the loaded world? The /summon command has no entity selector, and I don't want to go around writing down the coordinates of every creeper that I can see. The solution is the /execute command, arguably the most important command in the game because it is able to change the 'metadata' behind a command: who's running it, where they are, which direction they are facing, among other things. The /execute command has several different specifiers we can attach to it to make it run commands in different ways. One of these is the at specifier, which allows us to choose which entities we want to run some command at. In this case, we would want to do /execute at @e[type=minecraft:creeper] run summon minecraft:lightning_bolt ~ ~ ~ . This would run the command "summon a lightning bolt here" from the position of all of the creepers. It is very important to remember who is executing a command and where is the command being executed from. An example of the problems that happen when you forget this is the command /execute at @e[type=creeper] run kill @s . At first glance, this may seem like it will kill all creepers loaded in the world, but it won't. It will kill the entity who runs the command (assuming at least one creeper exists in the world), because @s refers to the self (kill self) and no matter where the command is executed (even if it is at the position of all creepers) @s still refers to whoever is running the command. A fix might appear to be /execute positioned as @e[type=creeper] run kill @s , but this has the same problem: the executing entity is still the entity who runs the command. To fix this, one would run /execute as @e[type=creeper] run kill @s . Now, @s refers to @e[type=creeper] . Of course, one could just do /kill @e[type=creeper] , but this is just an example problem. Item components This is all very well and good, but what if we want to do something more complicated, such as give a random player an unbreakable golden sword with Fire Aspect II which has the bolded, non-italic, dark-red name "Flame Boi" and eats non-gamers? This is where components come in. Components essentially allow you to set certain attributes of items beyond just their location. These consist of tags which have a name and a value . Sometimes, a tag may have multiple or nested values, in which case a list [] (series of values) or compound {} (tags within a tag) will be required. Components can support many other things, but right now we will just use the ones required for the sword. To give the sword, we would use /give @r golden_sword[enchantments={fire_aspect:2},unbreakable={},item_name={text:"Flame Boi",color:dark_red,italic:false,bold:true},lore=["This sword eats non-gamers."]] 1 To break it down, enchantments={...} is a list of enchantments, each of which has a key (the name of the enchantment) and a value (the level of the enchantment) The golden sword has the unbreakable component (the value doesn't matter but needs to be an object), so it lasts long enough to actually kill something. The item_name component specifies the name of the item in the inventory (another object specifying the item components) Finally, lore=[...] is a list of lines of lore to display. Each can be a string, or it can be an object using the same formatted text format as the item name. Additional component tips A very helpful command for learning about item components is /data get entity @s SelectedItem . It tells you all of the components that the item that you're currently holding has. That includes custom names, colors, enchantments, etc. To use it you can craft, find, or /give yourself the item that you want to use, rename and enchant it with an anvil and then hold it. Run /data get entity @s SelectedItem to get all of the components that the item has that you may need to /give yourself an identical item. When using /setblock or /summon rather than /give the syntax used is called NBT (Named Binary Tags) rather than components, and it works in a slightly different way but the same basic concepts still apply. A helpful keyboard shortcut is F3 + I , it will copy a /setblock or /summon command into your clipboard that you can use to set a block, or summon an entity that will be identical to the one you're looking at, including all NBT and block states. You can copy that command into a text editor with Ctrl + C to learn a lot about NBT. If you want a /summon command for a horse with blue leather armor, you can find or /summon a horse, give it blue leather armor, then look at it, press F3 + I and copy the command into a command block, no changes required. You won't need all of the NBT tags in most cases, you can make the command shorter by removing excess NBT tags. Make sure to test the command a few times in the process to make sure you didn't break anything. The keyboard shortcuts provided here are for Windows users, they may be different for mac, linux, or other systems Conclusion If you've read through this and still have a question on how a command works or where to put an NBT tag, item component, or something similar, be sure to read the wiki about that command, or this website which has the data types in NBT, this website which lists the item components in Minecraft, this website which contains information on player NBT, or this website which has information on chunk NBT. NBT and components use syntax very similar to JSON, so several links which may help explain JSON are this , this , this , this , and this . Don't worry if you don't have any programming knowledge/experience or if it is too technical for you: JSON is related to NBT and components in structure but you don't need to know about server-client data interchange or anything like that to use them. This is a good JSON validator, however be wary : JSON and NBT/components are not the same, so valid nbt may be flagged as incorrect JSON because the String identifiers are not enclosed with quotation marks. It's better to figure out why something is broken by hand (tracing braces/brackets, retyping it, checking capitalization...) than be misled by a JSON checker which operates by slightly different rules than NBT.
